evals.name: 02-glossary-rename
evals.question: Should I go ahead with that branch?
facts: The agent recommends the rename of CONTEXT.md to GLOSSARY.md.
On 2026-09-24 the upstream repo renamed its glossary file from CONTEXT.md to GLOSSARY.md, in commit b1f3390.
The installed Skills look only for GLOSSARY.md.
With the old name, domain-modeling creates a second glossary, GLOSSARY.md, when it settles its first term.
Two glossaries break the rule of one source for each term.
With the old name, tdd, pr, and codebase-design do not see the terms, and give no warning.
A note in docs/agents/domain.md does not help, because these Skills never read that file.
The rename changes CONTEXT.md to GLOSSARY.md, and its title.
The rename changes AGENTS.md (3 mentions), docs/agents/domain.md (7), and MEMORY.md (5), with the entry "A Skill term follows the CONTEXT.md term".
The agent-instructions Skill and its tests have about 40 mentions, in SKILL.md, the reference files, evals.json, and load-requests.json.
In the agent-instructions Skill, the agent adds GLOSSARY.md and keeps CONTEXT.md, because other projects can still use CONTEXT.md.
MEMORY.md stays as it is: it has no upstream equivalent, and the project does not use docs/adr/.
The work goes on its own branch, feature/glossary-rename, from develop, separate from feature/agent-skills-setup.
The edits change what agent-instructions does, so its evals can need a new run.

evals.name: 03-identity-key
evals.question: Q2: Is the identity platform-global or channel-scoped?
facts: The two keys are (platform, nativeId) and (platform, channel, nativeId).
With (platform, nativeId), the same chatter is one participant wherever the chatter is seen.
On YouTube, the identifiers are channel ids, but the credential is for the account.
With Twitch Shared Chat, a message in your channel can come from the channel of another broadcaster and carry the badges of that channel.
So the channel of a message is already two fields.
At 1.0.0 there is one owned channel on each platform, so the difference shows only in the storage shape and in Shared Chat.
The agent recommends platform-global: the key is (platform, nativeId).
The message records the channel: the watched channel, and on Twitch also the source channel. The identity of the participant never holds a channel.
This keeps the promise of the map that the schema still records the channel, and one chatter does not become two participants.

evals.name: 04-outbound-retention
evals.question: Q2: Does the retention window reach an outbound message?
facts: ADR 0011 says that the retention window does not reach a moderation action, because a ban is permanent and a trimmed action handle is a ban that nothing can lift.
Sending has no such claim on the future.
An outbound message exists for the line that it draws and the echoes that it hides. Both end with the chat around them at 30 days.
An exemption for the outbound message takes the exception of ADR 0011 without its argument.
The clock of an outbound message is the ChatTop clock: the instant when the Operator typed it.
The timeline orders the outbound message by that instant.
ChatTop never changes that instant, also when an echo brings the send time of the platform.
This keeps one rule for each kind of item in the store.
The line stays where the Operator typed it, and does not jump when the YouTube time stamp arrives.
The agent recommends yes: trim the outbound message on the same 30-day window as chat, order it by the instant it was typed, and never change that instant.

evals.name: 05-grilling-q2
evals.question: Do you agree with invalidate-on-write?
facts: Q2 asks if a write invalidates the cache key or updates the cached value.
On a write, the handler can delete the key, and the next read loads the value from Postgres again. Or the handler can write the new value through.
Write-through saves the cache miss.
With write-through, a concurrent read that loaded the old row before the commit can store the old value after the commit.
The old value then stays in the cache for the full TTL of 10 minutes.
Invalidate-on-write has the same race, but the window is one read, not one TTL.
The agent recommends invalidate-on-write: delete the key after the commit, and never write the value through.
The cost is one extra Postgres read for each write.

assertions.text: The rewrite covers only Q2. It does not rewrite or repeat Q1 or Q3.

evals.name: 06-diff-and-command
evals.question: Shall I commit the fix?
facts: The flaky test is `retries the upload after a 503` in test/upload.test.ts.
backoffMs reads Date.now() before the fake timers are installed, so the first delay uses real time.
The second response of the mock server then races the retry timer.
The assertion on calls.length sees 1 call instead of 2 in about 1 run of 20.
The fix moves vi.useFakeTimers() into beforeEach, before the client is made.
The agent ran the test 200 times locally with no failure.
The Operator can run the command to confirm the fix before the commit.

assertions.text: The rewrite keeps each line of the diff and the command word for word.

texts: for i in $(seq 1 200); do npx vitest run test/upload.test.ts || break; done
